newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire opposition leader promises reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Zaire opposition leader promises reconciliation.

text.p: Radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi returned home on Wednesday saying his symbolic handshake in France with Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko marked the start of national reconciliation.

Thousands of supporters of the one-time Mobutu friend turned rival came out to welcome Tshisekedi home from Europe after remarks he made there sparked a political furore and treason allegations at home.

Earlier, Zaire's transitional assembly, where Mobutu supporters enjoy a healthy majority, belatedly approved the October imposition of state of emergency in the east where Tutsi-led rebels now control towns and territory.

"The handshake marks the beginning of national reconciliation," Tshisekedi told well-wishers on arrival at Kinshasa's international airport, where several thousand supporters crowded the tarmac to welcome him.
"When Mobutu himself arrives in Kinshasa it is then that things will begin in earnest," he said, repeating that the solution to the revolt in the east was dialogue.
Thousands more supporters gathered along the road to Tshisekedi's Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UPDS) party headquarters at Limete 12 km (seven miles) away.

Tshisekedi said after "reconciliation" talks with Mobutu, who is recuperating from cancer surgery in southern France, that he had a mandate to form a government of national unity and called for dialogue with rebels in the east.
His remarks, in an interview on French radio, incensed the government of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, which said it had launched an inquiry into possible links between his party and the revolt.
"These irresponsible statements verge on treason and complicity with the enemy," government spokesman Boguo Makeli said in a televised account of last Friday's cabinet meeting.
Boguo, who repeatedly accused Rwanda of invading and backing the revolt, said Tshisekedi's party was the only Zairean political party with its flag flying in rebel-held territory.

Tshisekedi described the revolt in the east as an internal problem and played down Rwandan involvement. He said dialogue was the only solution with a role in Zaire for rebel leader Laurent Kabila, another arch-foe of Mobutu.
Mobutu, who seized power in a coup in 1965, has been absent from Zaire since he went to Switzerland for prostate surgery in August. His spokesman have for weeks said that his return was imminent.

Mobutu ruled virtually unchallenged until foreign and domestic pressure forced him to concede the principle of democratic reform in 1990 but Zaire's turbulent multi-party transition has dragged with repeated extensions in the life of the transitional parliament.
Under the transitional constitution, presidential and parliamentary elections must be held by July 1997. Mobutu has already said that he will stand.
The government imposed a state of emergency in North and South Kivu in October at the request of Mobutu and before much of the area fell to the rebels.

Parliament, which formally approved the measure with a show of hands on Tuesday, proposed that the army be given the means to win back the area and ensure security of neighbouring provinces. It also proposed a census of Rwandans and Burundians in Zaire.
